topics.title: Prefixes: mis-, in-, il-, im-, ir-, sub-, inter-, super-, anti-, auto-
topics.intro: A prefix changes a word’s meaning. in- means “not”, but it changes before some letters: il- before l (illegal), im- before m or p (impossible), ir- before r (irregular).
topics.talk: Ask {him} what a superhero, a submarine and an autopilot have to do with prefixes.

topics.title: Suffixes: -ation, -ly and -ous
topics.intro: Adding a suffix can change a word: happy → happily (y becomes i), gentle → gently (le becomes ly), basic → basically (-ic adds -ally), fame → famous (drop the e).
topics.teach: Explain how to add -ly to “gentle” and to “basic”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to turn “danger”, “fame” and “mountain” into -ous words.

topics.title: The “shun” endings: -tion, -sion, -ssion, -cian
topics.intro: Four ways to spell “shun”! Look at the root word: invent → invention (-tion), discuss → discussion (-ssion), expand → expansion (-sion), magic → magician (-cian, for jobs).
topics.talk: Ask {him} which ending a magician, an electrician and a musician all share.

topics.title: Unusual spellings: myth, young, chorus, chef, league, science, weigh
topics.intro: Some spellings come from other languages: y says “i” in myth and gym, ch says “k” in chorus and “sh” in chef, sc says “s” in science, and eigh says “ay” in weigh.
topics.teach: Explain three different sounds that “ch” can make.
topics.talk: Look for a “sc” word or a “ch-as-k” word on food packets or signs together.

topics.title: More homophones
topics.intro: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings. A car’s brake slows it down; a break is a rest (or a smash!).
topics.talk: Ask {him} to make up one sentence that uses both “meet” and “meat”.

topics.title: A or an, word families, vowels and consonants
topics.intro: Use “an” before a vowel SOUND (an astronaut, an hour) and “a” before a consonant sound (a rocket, a unicorn). Words in a family share a root: solve, solution, dissolve.
topics.teach: Explain why we say “an hour” but “a unicorn”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find three words in the “help” family.

topics.title: Joining words for time and cause; has and have
topics.intro: Conjunctions (when, before, after, while, so, because), adverbs (then, next, soon) and prepositions (before, after, during, because of) show WHEN and WHY things happen. “Has” and “have” make the present perfect: I have finished.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between “because” and “because of”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to tell you about {her} day using “before”, “after” and “while”.

topics.title: Clauses, paragraphs and speech
topics.intro: A clause is a group of words with a verb. A main clause makes sense on its own; a subordinate clause (because the engine was hot) needs a main clause. Paragraphs group ideas, and inverted commas show direct speech.
topics.teach: Explain what a subordinate clause is, with an example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} when a writer should start a new paragraph.

topics.title: Fronted adverbials
topics.intro: A fronted adverbial comes at the start of a sentence and tells you when, where or how: “Later that night, the robot woke up.” It is followed by a comma.
topics.teach: Explain where the comma goes after a fronted adverbial.
topics.talk: Take turns starting sentences with “Without a sound,” or “At midnight,”.

topics.title: Apostrophes for more than one owner
topics.intro: One driver’s helmet: the apostrophe goes before the s. Three drivers’ helmets: the plural already ends in s, so the apostrophe goes after it. But children’s and women’s add ’s.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between “the driver’s cars” and “the drivers’ cars”.
topics.talk: Find apostrophes on shop signs and decide: one owner or many?

topics.title: Standard English, determiners and pronouns
topics.intro: Standard English is the English we use in most writing and at school: “we were”, not “we was”; “I did”, not “I done”. Determiners (the, a, every, those) come before nouns. Pronouns (he, she, they) stop us repeating names, as long as it is clear who we mean.
topics.teach: Explain why “I seen it” is not Standard English.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to spot and fix “We was late!” in a silly voice.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Tie a ___ in the rope.”

options.feedback: “not” is the opposite of yes.

items.explain: knot has a silent k: a twist in rope.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The postman delivered the ___.”

options.feedback: “male” means a boy or man, or a male animal.

items.explain: mail = letters and parcels. male = boy or man.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The lion shook its ___.”

options.feedback: “main” means most important.

items.explain: mane = long hair on a lion’s or horse’s neck. main = most important.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Let’s ___ at the launch pad.”

options.feedback: meat is food from animals.

items.explain: meet = come together. meat = food.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Turbo won a gold ___.”

options.feedback: “meddle” means interfere in something that isn’t yours.

items.explain: medal = a prize. meddle = interfere.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “A thick ___ covered the track.”

options.feedback: “missed” is the past of miss: I missed the bus.

items.explain: mist = thin fog. missed = did not hit or catch.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Can I have a ___ of cake?”

options.feedback: “peace” means calm, with no war.

items.explain: A PIEce of PIE.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The ___ landed on the runway.”

options.feedback: “plain” means simple, or a flat area of land.

items.explain: plane = aeroplane. plain = simple, or flat land.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Queen Victoria’s ___ lasted 63 years.”

options.feedback: rain falls from clouds.
A rein is a strap for steering a horse.

items.explain: reign = the time a king or queen rules.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The knight pulled on his horse’s ___.”

options.feedback: rain falls from clouds.
A reign is the time a king or queen rules.

items.explain: rein = a strap used to steer a horse.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Have you ___ my helmet?”

options.feedback: A scene is a place or a part of a play.

items.explain: seen = past of see. scene = a place, or part of a play or film.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “I don’t know ___ we will win.”

options.feedback: weather is rain, sun and wind.

items.explain: whether = if. weather = rain, sun and wind.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “___ helmet is this?”

options.feedback: “Who’s” means “who is”: “Who is helmet is this?” doesn’t make sense.

items.explain: whose asks who something belongs to. who’s = who is.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “___ coming to the race?”

options.feedback: Try “Who is coming to the race?” It works, so use who’s.

items.explain: who’s = who is (or who has).

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.feedback: astronaut starts with a vowel sound, so use “an”.

items.explain: Use “an” before a vowel sound: an astronaut, an engine.

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.feedback: rocket starts with a consonant sound, so use “a”.

items.explain: Use “a” before a consonant sound.

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.feedback: The h in hour is silent, so the word starts with a vowel SOUND.

items.explain: It is the sound that matters: hour sounds like “our”, so “an hour”.

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.feedback: unicorn starts with a “y” sound (you-nicorn), which is a consonant sound.

items.explain: It is the sound that matters: “you-nicorn”, so “a unicorn”.

items.prompt: Choose a or an: “Bleep found ___ old map.”

options.feedback: old starts with a vowel sound.

items.explain: an old map.

items.prompt: Choose a or an: “{hero} spotted ___ huge asteroid.”

options.feedback: huge starts with a consonant sound (h), so use “a”.

items.explain: The a/an choice depends on the very next word: a huge asteroid, an asteroid.

items.prompt: Which word is in the same word family as “solve”?
items.explain: Word families share a root and a meaning: solve, solution, solver, dissolve.

items.prompt: Which word is in the same word family as “help”?
items.explain: help, helpful, helpless, helper: they all share the meaning of help.

items.prompt: Which word belongs to the “sign” family?
items.explain: sign, signal, signature: the g is silent in sign, but you can hear it in signature. Word families help with spelling!

items.prompt: Which word belongs to the same family as “telephone” (phone means sound)?
items.explain: telephone, microphone, headphones: phone means sound.

items.prompt: How many vowel letters are there: a, e, i, o, u?
items.explain: The other 21 letters are consonants. (The letter y sometimes acts like a vowel too, as in “gym”.)

items.prompt: Is the letter “t” a vowel or a consonant?
items.explain: a, e, i, o and u are vowels. All the other letters are consonants.

items.prompt: Which word starts with a vowel?

options.feedback: t is a consonant.
w is a consonant.
b is a consonant.

items.explain: engine starts with e, a vowel, so it is “an engine”.

items.prompt: What is the root word of “unhelpful”?
items.explain: Take away the prefix un- and the suffix -ful: help.

items.prompt: What is the root word of “disappearing”?
items.explain: Take away the prefix dis- and the suffix -ing: appear.

items.prompt: Choose the best conjunction: “Put on your helmet ___ you start the engine.”

options.feedback: Safety first: the helmet goes on first.
“because” gives a reason, which doesn’t fit here.

items.explain: “before” shows which thing happens first.

items.prompt: Choose the best conjunction: “{hero} had a long rest ___ the battle was won.”

options.feedback: You rest when the battle is over, not before.
“although” shows a surprise, which doesn’t fit.

items.explain: “after” shows the rest came later.

items.prompt: Choose the best conjunction: “Turbo waited ___ the mechanics changed his tyres.”

options.feedback: “so” shows a result.
“because” gives a reason. This sentence is about two things happening at the same time.

items.explain: “while” shows two things happening at the same time.

items.prompt: Choose the best conjunction: “It was pouring with rain, ___ the race was stopped.”

options.feedback: Try it: “It was raining because the race was stopped” gets the cause the wrong way round.
This is about cause and result, not time.

items.explain: “so” shows the result.

items.prompt: Choose the best conjunction: “The race was stopped ___ it was pouring with rain.”

options.feedback: “so” would mean the rain was caused by stopping the race!
The point is WHY it stopped.

items.explain: “because” gives the reason (the cause).

items.prompt: Which of these is an adverb that tells you WHEN?

options.feedback: “because” is a conjunction.
“under” is a preposition of place.
“quickly” tells you HOW.

items.explain: Time adverbs: then, next, soon, later, afterwards.

items.prompt: Fill the gap: “First, check the fuel. ___, start the engine.”

options.feedback: “Because” needs a reason after it.
“Under” is about place.

items.explain: Time adverbs like First, Next and Then order instructions.

items.prompt: Which word is a preposition? “The robot hid under the table.”

options.feedback: robot is a noun.
hid is a verb.
table is a noun.

items.explain: Prepositions show where or when something is: under, over, during, before.

items.prompt: Which preposition tells you WHEN? “We watched a film ___ the storm.”

options.feedback: “under” tells you where.
“beside” tells you where.

items.explain: “during” means while something was happening.

items.prompt: Which fits? “The match was stopped ___ the rain.”

options.feedback: “because” needs a whole clause after it: because it rained.
“so” shows a result.

items.explain: “because of” is followed by a noun: because of the rain.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the present perfect (has or have + verb)?

options.text: Captain Nova has landed on Mars.

options.feedback: That is the simple past.

options.text: Captain Nova will land on Mars.
options.feedback: That is the future.

items.explain: The present perfect (has landed) shows something that happened and still matters now.

items.prompt: Fill the gap: “I ___ my homework, so now I can play.”

options.feedback: The homework is already done, and it matters now.
If it was still to do, you couldn’t play yet!

items.explain: have finished: done, and that matters now.

items.prompt: Present perfect: “She ___ (go) to the shops.”
items.explain: has gone, never has went. (“Went” is used on its own: she went.)

items.prompt: Present perfect: “They ___ (eat) all the biscuits!”
items.explain: they have eaten, never have ate.

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.feedback: After has, use written: has written.
With he, use has.

items.explain: he has written; they have written.

items.prompt: What is a conjunction?

options.text: A word that joins clauses, like “because”

options.feedback: That is a noun.
That is an adjective.

items.explain: Conjunctions join: and, but, or, so, because, when, while, if.

items.prompt: What is a clause?

options.text: A group of words with a verb in it

options.feedback: A clause is a group of words.

options.text: A capital letter and a full stop
options.feedback: Those are punctuation.

items.explain: A clause has a verb (and usually someone doing it): Turbo won.

items.prompt: In “Turbo won the race because he practised”, which is the main clause?

options.feedback: This can’t make sense on its own: it is the subordinate clause.
Who won? Without “Turbo” this doesn’t make sense on its own.

items.explain: The main clause makes sense on its own: Turbo won the race.

items.prompt: In “When the lights turned green, Rosa pressed the pedal”, which is the subordinate clause?

options.feedback: That makes sense on its own: it is the main clause.
That has no verb, so it isn’t a clause.

items.explain: A subordinate clause starts with a word like when, because or if, and needs the main clause.

items.prompt: Which is a subordinate clause (it can’t make sense on its own)?

options.feedback: That makes sense on its own.
That makes sense on its own.

items.explain: “because the engine was hot…” leaves you waiting for more.

items.prompt: Which sentence has a subordinate clause?

options.text: {hero} flew home after the storm ended.
{hero} flew home and the storm ended.
options.feedback: Two main clauses joined by “and”: neither depends on the other.
Just one clause here: “through the storm” has no verb.

items.explain: “after the storm ended” is the subordinate clause.

items.prompt: Why do writers use paragraphs?

options.text: To group sentences about one idea
To make the writing look longer
options.feedback: Paragraphs organise writing; they don’t make it longer.

options.text: Because every sentence needs a new line
options.feedback: A paragraph usually has several sentences.

items.explain: A new paragraph tells the reader: something has changed.

items.prompt: In a fact file about the planets, what are headings for?

options.text: To show what each part is about
To make it look more like a story
options.feedback: Stories don’t usually have headings.

options.text: To show where a sentence ends
options.feedback: That is a full stop’s job.

items.explain: Headings and subheadings help readers find information quickly.

items.prompt: When should you start a new paragraph in a story?

options.text: When the time, place or speaker changes
After every single sentence you write
options.feedback: That would be very bitty!

options.text: Only once, right at the very end
options.feedback: Paragraphs are for the whole story.

items.explain: Remember TiPToP: a new paragraph for a new Time, Place, Topic or Person.

items.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?

options.feedback: Only the spoken words go inside the inverted commas.
“said” carries on the same sentence, so it doesn’t need a capital.

items.explain: The ! goes inside the inverted commas, and “said” has a small s.

items.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?

options.text: Captain Nova said, “We land at dawn.”
Captain Nova said, “we land at dawn.”
options.feedback: The spoken words start with a capital letter.

options.text: Captain Nova said “We land at dawn”.
options.feedback: Use a comma before the speech, and put the full stop inside.

items.explain: Comma, open inverted commas, capital letter, words, full stop, close inverted commas.

items.prompt: What is another name for speech marks?

options.feedback: Apostrophes show missing letters or belonging.
Brackets look like ( ).

items.explain: Speech marks are called inverted commas: they look like upside-down commas.

items.prompt: What do we call the exact words someone says, written inside inverted commas?

options.feedback: A heading is a title for a section.
A prefix goes at the start of a word.

items.explain: “Blast off!” is direct speech.

items.prompt: In a story, what should you do when a new person starts speaking?

options.text: Use capital letters for every word
options.feedback: Just the first word of the speech has a capital.
Every speaker’s words go in inverted commas.

items.explain: New speaker, new line: it helps the reader know who is talking.

items.prompt: What is a prefix?

options.text: Letters added to the start of a word
Letters added to the end of a word
options.feedback: That is a suffix.

options.text: A word that joins two clauses
options.feedback: That is a conjunction.

items.explain: un-, dis-, re- and super- are prefixes.

items.prompt: What is “un-” in “unhappy”?

options.feedback: Suffixes go at the end.
Conjunctions are joining words.

items.explain: un- is a prefix meaning not.

items.prompt: What is a fronted adverbial?

options.text: A word or phrase at the start saying when, where or how
The very last word in a sentence
options.feedback: “Fronted” means at the front.
That is a noun.

items.explain: Later that night, Behind the wall, Without a sound: these are fronted adverbials.

items.prompt: Which sentence starts with a fronted adverbial?

options.text: Later that night, the robot woke up.
The robot woke up later that night.
options.feedback: The adverbial is at the end here, not the front.
There is no adverbial here.

items.explain: “Later that night” has moved to the front, followed by a comma.

items.prompt: Where does the comma go?

options.text: As fast as lightning, Turbo zoomed past.
As fast, as lightning Turbo zoomed past.
options.feedback: The comma goes after the whole adverbial.

options.text: As fast as lightning Turbo, zoomed past.
options.feedback: The comma goes before Turbo, where the adverbial ends.

items.explain: The comma comes straight after the fronted adverbial.

items.prompt: Which fronted adverbial tells you WHERE?

options.feedback: That tells you how.
That tells you when.

items.explain: Behind the castle wall tells you the place.

items.prompt: Which fronted adverbial tells you HOW?

options.feedback: That tells you when.
That tells you where.

items.explain: Without a sound tells you how it was done.

items.prompt: Which fronted adverbial tells you WHEN?

options.feedback: That tells you where.
That tells you how.

items.explain: At midnight tells you the time.

items.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?

options.feedback: The comma goes right after “Suddenly”.
The comma goes right after “Suddenly”.

items.explain: One-word fronted adverbials need a comma too: Suddenly, …

items.prompt: Choose the best fronted adverbial: “___, the knights charged across the field.”

options.feedback: You can’t charge while fast asleep!
“Because” needs a reason after it.

items.explain: With a mighty roar tells you HOW they charged.

items.prompt: ONE driver owns a helmet. Which is correct?

options.feedback: That would mean more than one driver.
You need an apostrophe to show belonging.

items.explain: One owner: ’s. the driver’s helmet.

items.prompt: THREE drivers each own a helmet. Which is correct?

options.feedback: That means one driver with several helmets.
The apostrophe shows who owns, so it goes on drivers.

items.explain: The plural “drivers” already ends in s, so just add the apostrophe after it: drivers’.

items.prompt: Which shows cars belonging to MORE THAN ONE racer?

options.feedback: That is one racer.
The apostrophe goes on the owners, not the cars.

items.explain: racers + ’ = racers’.

items.prompt: Which is correct? (The toys belong to the children.)

options.feedback: children doesn’t end in s, so add ’s.
You need an apostrophe.

items.explain: Plurals that don’t end in s add ’s: children’s, women’s, men’s.

items.prompt: Which is correct? (The team belongs to the women.)

options.feedback: women doesn’t end in s, so add ’s.
You need an apostrophe.

items.explain: women + ’s = women’s.

items.prompt: Which means the tails of SEVERAL dogs?

options.feedback: That is one dog with lots of tails!
The apostrophe goes on the owners.

items.explain: Several dogs: dogs’.

items.prompt: Which is correct? (The nests of the birds.)

options.feedback: That is one bird with several nests.
The apostrophe goes on the owners.

items.explain: birds + ’ = birds’.

items.prompt: Which is correct? (The cloaks of the men.)

options.feedback: men doesn’t end in s, so add ’s.
You need an apostrophe.

items.explain: men + ’s = men’s.

items.prompt: Which sentence needs NO apostrophe?

options.feedback: The suits belong to the astronauts: astronauts’ suits.
This one already has one, correctly: the helmet belongs to the astronaut.

items.explain: A plain plural (astronauts) never needs an apostrophe.

items.prompt: Which is Standard English?

options.text: They were tired after the race.
They was tired after the race.
options.feedback: With they, use were.

items.explain: I was, you were, he was, we were, they were.

items.prompt: Which is Standard English?

options.feedback: “done” needs a helper: I have done. On its own, use did.

items.explain: I did it. I have done it.

items.prompt: Which is Standard English?

options.feedback: “seen” needs a helper: I have seen. On its own, use saw.

items.explain: I saw it. I have seen it.

items.prompt: Which is Standard English?

options.feedback: “them” can’t go before a noun. Use those.

items.explain: those rockets, not them rockets.

items.prompt: Which is Standard English?

options.feedback: That uses two negatives (haven’t + no). Standard English uses only one: haven’t got any.

items.explain: Use only one negative: haven’t got any, or have got none.

items.prompt: Which word is the determiner? “The robot danced.”

options.feedback: robot is a noun.
danced is a verb.

items.explain: Determiners come before nouns: the, a, an, this, those, every, some.

items.prompt: Which of these words is a determiner?

options.feedback: quickly is an adverb.
jump is a verb.
happy is an adjective.

items.explain: every robot, every day: “every” is a determiner.

items.prompt: Which uses a pronoun to avoid repeating a name?

options.text: Bleep opened the box. He found a crystal inside.
Bleep opened the box. Bleep found a crystal inside.
options.feedback: This repeats “Bleep”.

options.text: Bleep opened the box. Box found a crystal inside.
options.feedback: That changes the meaning!

items.explain: “He” stands for Bleep, so we don’t repeat the name.

items.prompt: In “Rosa grabbed the wheel gun. She worked fast.”, who is “She”?

options.feedback: A wheel gun isn’t a “she”.
Captain Nova isn’t in these sentences.

items.explain: Pronouns point back to a noun that came before.

items.prompt: Why might a writer use a name again instead of a pronoun?

options.text: To make it clear who is meant

options.feedback: Pronouns are useful; they just need to be clear.
A name is usually longer than a pronoun.

items.explain: “Turbo and Blaze raced. He won.” Who won? Using the name makes it clear.

items.prompt: Which word is a pronoun?

options.feedback: rocket is a noun.
zoom is a verb.
fast is an adjective or adverb.

items.explain: Pronouns stand in for nouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.

sentences.title: Has or have
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence about something you have done this week, using “has” or “have”.
sentences.model: I have finished my space project.
sentences.tip: has or have + a verb shows something that is done and still matters now.

sentences.title: Use “while”
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence using “while” to show two things happening at the same time.

checks.msg: Write about both things that are happening.

sentences.model: Turbo waited in the pit lane while the crew changed his tyres.
sentences.tip: “while” joins two things happening at once.

sentences.title: A or an
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that uses “an” correctly, like “an astronaut” or “an engine”.

checks.msg: Use “an” before a word starting with a vowel.

sentences.model: Bleep found an old map in the cave.
sentences.tip: Use “an” before a vowel sound: an astronaut, an hour.

sentences.title: Speech, punctuated
sentences.prompt: Write what Captain Nova shouts when she spots an alien. Use inverted commas, start the speech with a capital, and put ! or a comma before the closing inverted commas.

checks.msg: Start the speech with a capital, and put , ! or ? just before the closing inverted commas.

sentences.tip: The punctuation that ends the speech goes inside the inverted commas.

sentences.title: A fronted adverbial
sentences.prompt: Start a sentence about a knight with a fronted adverbial (like “At midnight,” or “Without a sound,”) followed by a comma.

checks.msg: Start with a fronted adverbial, then a comma.
Finish the sentence: what did the knight do?

sentences.model: Without a sound, the knight crept into the castle.
sentences.tip: The comma goes straight after the fronted adverbial.

sentences.title: Start with a subordinate clause
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that starts with “When”, “After” or “Before”, with a comma after the first part.

checks.msg: Start with When, After or Before, and put a comma after the first part.
Write both parts of the sentence.

sentences.model: When the rocket landed, the crowd cheered.
sentences.tip: The subordinate clause comes first, then a comma, then the main clause.

sentences.title: A “not” prefix
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence using one of these words: impossible, invisible, incorrect, illegal or irregular.

checks.msg: Use one of the five words.

sentences.tip: in-, im-, il- and ir- all mean “not”.

sentences.title: Use “because of”
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence using “because of”, like “The race was stopped because of the rain.”
sentences.model: The rocket launch was delayed because of the storm.
sentences.tip: “because of” is followed by a noun: because of the storm.
